Composing {{math|''f''}}, and hence {{math|''F''}}, with complex conjugation if necessary, it can further be assumed that {{math|''F''}} preserves the orientation of the circle. In this case, if {{math|''a'',''b'', ''c'',''d''}} are in order on the circle, so too are there images under {{math|''F''}}; hence both {{math|(''a'',''b'';''c'',''d'')}} and {{math|(''F''(''a''),''F''(''b'');''F''(''c''),''F''(''d''))}} are real and greater than one. In this case

<math display=block>(F(a),F(b);F(c),F(d)) \le A (a,b;c,d)^B.</math>

To prove this, it suffices to show that {{math|1=log (''F''(''a''),''F''(''b'');''F''(''c''),''F''(''d'')) ≤ ''B'' log (''a'',''b'';''c'',''d'') + ''C''}}. From the previous section it suffices show {{math|1=''d''([''F''(''a''),''F''(''b'')],[''F''(''c''),''F''(''d'')]) ≤ ''P'' ''d''([''a'',''b''],[''c'',''d'']) + ''Q''}}. This follows from the fact that the images under {{math|''f''}} of {{math|[''a'',''b'']}} and {{math|[''c'',''d'']}} lie within {{math|''h''}}-neighbourhoods of {{math|[''F''(''a''),''F''(''b'')]}} and {{math|[''F''(''c''),''F''(''d'')]}}; the minimal distance can be estimated using the quasi-isometry constants for {{math|''f''}} applied to the points on {{math|[''a'',''b'']}} and {{math|[''c'',''d'']}}
realising {{math|''d''([''a'',''b''],[''c'',''d''])}}.

Adjusting {{math|''A''}} and {{math|''B''}} if necessary, the inequality above applies also to {{math|''F''<sup>−1</sup>}}. Replacing {{math|''a''}}, {{math|''b''}}, {{math|''c''}} and {{math|''d''}} by their images under {{math|''F''}}, it follows that

<math display=block>A^{-1} |(a,b;c,d)|^{-B} \le |(F(a),F(b);F(c),F(d))| \le A |(a,b;c,d)|^B</math>

if {{math|''a''}}, {{math|''b''}}, {{math|''c''}} and {{math|''d''}} are in order on the unit circle. Hence the same inequalities are valid for the three cyclic of the quadruple {{math|''a'', ''b'', ''c'', ''d''}}. If {{math|''a''}} and {{math|''b''}} are switched then the cross ratios are sent to their inverses, so lie between 0 and 1; similarly if {{math|''c''}} and {{math|''d''}} are switched. If both pairs are switched, the cross ratio remains unaltered.  Hence the inequalities are also valid in this case. Finally if {{math|''b''}} and {{math|''c''}} are interchanged, the cross ratio changes from {{math|λ}} to {{math|1=λ<sup>–1</sup>
(λ – 1) = 1 – λ<sup>–1</sup>}}, which lies between 0 and 1. Hence again the same inequalities are valid. It is easy to check that using these transformations the inequalities are valid for all possible permutations of {{math|''a''}}, {{math|''b''}}, {{math|''c''}} and {{math|''d''}}, so that {{math|''F''}} and its inverse are quasi-Möbius homeomorphisms.

== Busemann functions and visual metrics for CAT(-1) spaces==

Busemann functions can be used to determine special visual metrics on the class of CAT(-1) spaces. These are complete geodesic metric spaces in which the distances between points on the boundary of a geodesic triangle are less than or equal to the comparison triangle in the hyperbolic upper half plane or equivalently the unit disk with the Poincaré metric. In the case of the unit disk the chordal metric can be recovered directly using Busemann functions {{math|''B''<sub>γ</sub>}} and the special theory for the disk generalises completely to any proper CAT(-1) space {{math|''X''}}. The hyperbolic upper half plane is a CAT(0) space, as lengths in a hyperbolic geodesic triangle are less than lengths in the Euclidean comparison triangle: in particular a CAT(-1) space is a CAT(0) space, so the theory of Busemann functions and the Gromov boundary applies. From the theory of the hyperbolic disk, it follows in particular that every geodesic ray in a CAT(-1) space extends to a geodesic line and given two points of the boundary there is a unique geodesic {{math|γ}} such that has these points as the limits {{math|γ(±∞)}}. The theory applies equally well to any CAT({{math|−κ}}) space with {{math|κ > 0}} since these arise by scaling the metric on a CAT(-1) space by {{math|κ<sup>−1/2</sup>}}. On the hyperbolic unit disk {{math|''D''}} quasi-isometries of {{math|''D''}} induce quasi-Möbius homeomorphisms of the boundary in a functorial way. There is a more general theory of Gromov hyperbolic spaces, a similar statement holds, but with less precise control on the homeomorphisms of the boundary.<ref name="Bourdon 1995"/><ref name="Buyalo 2007"/>

===Example: Poincaré disk===

==Applications in percolation theory==
{{further|percolation theory}}
More recently Busemann functions have been used by [[probability theory|probabilists]] to study asymptotic properties in models of [[first passage percolation|first-passage percolation]]<ref>{{harvnb|Hoffman|2005}}</ref><ref>{{harvnb|Damron|Hanson|2014}}</ref> and directed last-passage percolation.<ref>{{harvnb|Georgiou|Rassoul-Agha|Seppäläinen|2016}}</ref>
